vignette:
She is 67, a South Asian woman who has spent most of her adult life working for non-profit organizations, the kind of person who remembers donors’ names, brings food to meetings, and stays late to help a young colleague finish a grant application. She is married, a mother and grandmother, and in many parts of her life she is seen as steady, dignified, and deeply reliable. When she speaks about what happened to her, though, her voice changes. It becomes quieter, flatter, as if she is stepping carefully around something sharp.

The assault happens late in her fifties, during a period when her work has her moving constantly between community events, fundraising dinners, and meetings with partner agencies. She has built a reputation for being warm and collaborative, and she prides herself on being able to put people at ease. The man who assaults her is someone she knows through work, someone who is familiar enough that she does not initially feel danger. She remembers the room in pieces afterward: the smell of stale coffee, the scrape of a chair, the sudden feeling that her body is no longer fully hers. What remains most vivid is not only fear but disbelief. Even as it is happening, part of her mind keeps insisting that there must be some mistake, that if she says the right thing or shifts her tone, this version of reality will stop.

In the days after, she tells no one. She goes home to her husband and moves through the evening as if she is acting in a play she has rehearsed for years. She serves dinner, asks about errands, folds laundry. Inside, she feels contaminated and strangely absent. When she showers, she scrubs herself hard enough to leave her skin raw. At night she lies awake, then startles when she does drift off. Sleep brings jagged, repetitive dreams in which she is trapped, voiceless, or trying to run through thick water. She begins to dread bedtime.

She does not report the assault. The reasons are many and tangled. She worries she will not be believed. She worries about shame, about what it would mean in her family and community to speak aloud what was done to her. She is furious with herself for having trusted him, for not having fought harder, though another part of her knows how frozen she became. She starts replaying the event constantly, examining each second as if she might still find the moment where she could have changed the outcome.

At work, the impact spreads quietly. She continues performing well enough that others do not immediately notice, but the effort is enormous. She avoids being alone with men she does not know well. She changes routes through office buildings, checks door locks repeatedly, and positions herself near exits during meetings. If a male colleague stands too close behind her, her heart races and her muscles go rigid before she even has time to think. She becomes exquisitely alert to tone of voice, footsteps in hallways, the sound of a door closing. Community events that once energized her now feel dangerous and exhausting. She smiles through them, then goes home and sits in her car in the driveway, unable to make herself go inside.

Her husband knows something is wrong long before he knows anything specific. He notices that she startles when he enters a room unexpectedly. He notices she no longer likes being touched without warning, even affectionately. Their marriage becomes strained not because she loves him less, but because closeness now feels unpredictable. She wants comfort and simultaneously recoils from it. Sometimes she snaps at him for small things and then feels ashamed. Sometimes she says nothing at all for hours. She describes feeling as if a pane of glass has come down between her and everyone else.

Over the years, she narrows her life. She declines invitations, especially evening events. She stops traveling alone for work. She tells herself she is simply getting older, more private, less social, but privately she knows she is organizing her days around not being triggered. The assault returns in flashes: a certain cologne, a news story, a fundraising venue with dim carpeting and conference chairs. In those moments she is no longer remembering; she is there again, breath shallow, body tense, mind emptied of everything except danger. Afterwards she feels embarrassed by the intensity of her reaction and angry that so much time has passed without relief.

She also carries a heavy burden of self-blame. She wonders whether her friendliness was misread, whether her professional openness somehow invited harm. She feels guilty for not speaking sooner and for the ways her silence has shaped her marriage and work. Yet beneath that guilt is grief—for the ease she once had in the world, for the version of herself who could walk into a room without first scanning it.

Now, years later, she still wakes from sleep with her heart pounding. She still checks locks more than once. In conversation she can seem composed, but if she gets close to certain details her hands tremble and her gaze shifts to the door. She says she is tired of being governed by something she did not choose. What pains her most is not only the memory of the assault itself, but the long aftermath: how thoroughly it has altered her sense of safety, intimacy, and trust in her own body.
